covered: Earning versus collection; expense versus payment; receivables, accruals, prepayments and customer advances; a reconciled profit-to-cash comparison.
deferred: Complete statutory cash-basis rules, tax eligibility, complex contracts, depreciation schedules and full cash-flow classification.

hoverDefinition: Accrual accounting records economic performance when it occurs. Cash-based records follow receipts and payments. The timing difference is carried in balances such as receivables, payables, prepayments and customer advances.

objectives.statement: Calculate period profit and operating cash movement from separate earning, collection, expense and payment data.
objectives.evidence: Reconcile the difference using closing customer and supplier/employee balances.

objectives.statement: Allocate a prepaid cost and a partly fulfilled customer advance to the current period.
objectives.evidence: Separate expense from prepaid asset and revenue from the remaining contract liability.

context.timeframe: A separate illustrative teaching month. Every worked example and practice scenario starts independently; these are not consecutive company-case rounds.
assumptions: All stated revenue and expenses satisfy the simplified recognition assumptions.
Insurance coverage is consumed equally each month.
No tax, interest, depreciation, impairment or unmentioned operating balance.
The cash-basis comparison includes stated operating receipts and payments only.

framework.limitations: Simplified conceptual teaching example. Recognition and amounts are explicitly assumed; no claim of compliance with a jurisdiction-specific reporting or tax regime.

mechanism.title: Follow the performance clock and the cash clock
paragraphs: A qualifying delivery can earn revenue in one period and be collected in another. Consuming a resource or receiving employee service can create an expense before payment. Accrual accounting records those economic effects in their own periods and carries the unpaid amounts as balances.

A simple cash-basis comparison follows operating money received and paid. In this lesson its result is called an operating cash surplus. It is not a universal legal cash-basis income calculation: borrowing and owner contributions are funding, and equipment purchases need their own treatment.

mechanism.title: Identify amounts earned or incurred but unsettled
paragraphs: Trade receivables track recognised customer claims that remain unpaid. An accrued wage expense creates an obligation for service already received. Later collection or payment settles the balance; it does not repeat the original revenue or expense.

For a simple period with no other adjustments, profit minus an increase in receivables plus an increase in unpaid operating costs approaches operating cash. Each adjustment must use the same period and a consistent balance definition. Add inventory and prepaid movements when those exist.

mechanism.title: Identify cash that arrives before performance
paragraphs: A payment for coverage extending into future months initially creates a prepaid asset under the stated assumptions. The consumed portion becomes expense. A customer advance creates an obligation to perform; it becomes revenue only as the promised goods or services are transferred under the contract.

Do not force an expense merely to match a sales number. Recognition follows the resource consumed or obligation incurred. The illustrations assume equal insurance coverage per month, and specified customer performance; actual contracts can require a different pattern.

mechanism.title: Reconcile before drawing a conclusion
paragraphs: Begin with actual receipts and payments to calculate operating cash movement. Calculate accrual profit independently, then bridge the two using changes in operating balances. Exclude funding receipts from operating income. A business can report a profit while customers still owe it money or while it pays for resources used in future periods.

distinctions.name: Accrued income and customer receipt
distinctions.explanation: Income may be recognised before or after cash collection, depending on the performance.
distinctions.whenItMatters: A bank receipt alone does not establish current revenue.

distinctions.name: Accrued expense and settlement
distinctions.explanation: The cost of service received can precede its payment.
distinctions.whenItMatters: Paying a previously recorded expense does not create it again.

distinctions.name: Prepaid asset and consumed expense
distinctions.explanation: The unconsumed right is an asset; the period’s consumed part is expense.
distinctions.whenItMatters: A multi-period payment should not automatically be charged entirely to one month.

distinctions.name: Customer advance and revenue
distinctions.explanation: An advance carries an unfulfilled promise until the stated performance occurs.
distinctions.whenItMatters: Cash can improve while the business still owes goods or services.

distinctions.name: Operating cash surplus and total cash change
distinctions.explanation: Borrowing, capital injections and equipment payments can affect cash without being current operating income or expense.
distinctions.whenItMatters: Label the cash perimeter before comparing it with profit.

workedExample.setup: Separate month: opening cash is 20 and inventory is 12, funded by opening equity 32. Nila delivers all that inventory in qualifying credit sales of 30 and collects 18. Wages of 6 are incurred, of which 4 are paid. It also pays 6 for three equal months of insurance beginning this month. No other events or balances exist.

inputs.label: Opening inventory, all sold this month

steps: Revenue is 30; the 12 carrying cost of inventory sold is expense.
Wage expense is 6 even though only 4 is paid. Wages payable close at 2.
Insurance expense = 6 ÷ 3 = 2; the remaining prepaid asset is 4.
Operating cash movement = receipts 18 − wages paid 4 − insurance paid 6 = +8. Closing cash is 20 + 8 = 28.
Bridge from profit: 10 − receivables increase 12 + inventory decrease 12 + wages payable increase 2 − prepaid increase 4 = 8.
Closing assets = cash 28 + receivables 12 + prepaid insurance 4 = 44. Liabilities 2 + equity (32 + profit 10) 42 = 44.
workedExample.result: Accrual profit is 10; operating cash movement is +8; cash closes at 28.
workedExample.interpretation: The inventory payment occurred before this month, some wages remain unpaid and some insurance is unconsumed. Every timing difference must be included before interpreting the two totals.

statementEffects.explanation: These are complete simplified operating movements for this separate example, excluding tax, financing, investments and other non-cash items.
changes: Income statement: revenue 30; inventory expense 12, wage expense 6 and insurance expense 2; profit 10.
Balance sheet: cash 28, receivables 12, prepaid insurance 4, wages payable 2 and equity 42.
Cash flow: current customer receipts 18 less current operating payments 10 gives +8.

misconceptions.claim: Current profit is simply money received minus all money paid.
misconceptions.correction: Identify earned revenue, consumed resources, operating balances and funding separately.
misconceptions.diagnostic: What did the business earn or consume this period?

misconceptions.claim: A payment covering future months is entirely this month’s expense.
misconceptions.correction: Allocate the consumed coverage under the stated assumption and retain the rest as an asset.
misconceptions.diagnostic: How much service is still owed to the business?

misconceptions.claim: A customer advance is already earned revenue.
misconceptions.correction: The unperformed portion remains an obligation.

practice.setup: Separate Nila installation-service example: all service qualifying for revenue of 24 is completed this month, and customers pay 9. Wage service of 7 is received, with 5 paid. There is no inventory, tax, prepayment or other event and no opening operating balances.
practice.question: What are accrual profit and operating cash movement?

options.feedback: 4 is the operating cash result. Revenue and expense timing still need recognition.
Profit is 24 − 7. Cash is 9 − 5; receivables 15 and wages payable 2 explain the gap.
Recognised income is not the same as collected money.

practice.solution: Profit = 24 − 7 = 17. Operating cash = 9 − 5 = 4. Bridge: 17 − receivables increase 15 + wages payable increase 2 = 4.

hints.text: Compute the performance result and the bank movements independently.
Profit = 24 − 7 = 17. Operating cash = 9 − 5 = 4. Bridge: 17 − receivables increase 15 + wages payable increase 2 = 4.

reflection.prompt: Why can this service be profitable before the customers settle?

practice.setup: Separate scenario: pay 12 for six equal months of insurance beginning now. Receive a customer advance of 8 and complete the part of the promise allocated a price of 3 this month. No other expenses, receipts or payments occur. The unfulfilled promise is still owed; no receivable arises.
practice.question: Which current-month result and closing balances follow?

options.text: Loss 9; prepaid asset 0; customer liability 5; cash −4
options.feedback: Only 2 of insurance coverage is consumed this month.

options.text: Profit 6; prepaid asset 10; customer liability 0; cash −4
options.feedback: The unfulfilled portion 5 remains an obligation.

options.text: Profit 1; prepaid asset 10; customer liability 5; cash −4
options.feedback: Revenue 3 less insurance expense 2 gives profit 1; cash is 8 − 12.

practice.solution: Insurance expense = 12 ÷ 6 = 2; prepaid asset = 10. Revenue = 3; customer liability = 8 − 3 = 5. Profit = 1. Cash movement = 8 − 12 = −4. Bridge: profit 1 − prepaid increase 10 + customer liability increase 5 = −4.

hints.text: Separate the part consumed or performed from the future portion of each payment.

Insurance expense = 12 ÷ 6 = 2; prepaid asset = 10. Revenue = 3; customer liability = 8 − 3 = 5. Profit = 1. Cash movement = 8 − 12 = −4. Bridge: profit 1 − prepaid increase 10 + customer liability increase 5 = −4.

reflection.prompt: How do the two future obligations explain profit exceeding cash movement?
